title: Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP)
summary: A rare, slow-growing skin sarcoma that starts as a firm plaque, often on the trunk, and is easily mistaken for a scar, keloid or dermatofibroma. It rarely spreads but recurs locally unless widely excised (often Mohs).

glance.think: A firm, slowly enlarging plaque on the trunk or shoulder that later becomes lumpy (protuberant).
glance.engine: A low-grade fibroblastic sarcoma driven by a COL1A1–PDGFB gene fusion.
glance.backbone: Refer on a suspected sarcoma or skin-cancer pathway; deep biopsy; Mohs or wide excision; imatinib for inoperable disease.
glance.never_miss: Delayed diagnosis because it is called a scar, keloid or dermatofibroma for years.

what: A rare, locally aggressive, low-grade **cutaneous sarcoma**. It infiltrates widely beneath clinically normal skin ("tentacles") and recurs if under-excised. Metastasis is rare (<5%) and mostly follows fibrosarcomatous transformation or repeated recurrence.

list: Over 90% carry the translocation **t(17;22)** (often as a ring chromosome), fusing **COL1A1–PDGFB**. This drives autocrine PDGF receptor stimulation and is the rationale for **imatinib** in unresectable or metastatic disease.
Histology: storiform spindle cells infiltrating fat in a "honeycomb" pattern; **CD34 positive, Factor XIIIa negative** (contrast DF).
Adults aged 20–50; trunk (especially chest and shoulder), proximal limbs, head and neck.

Starts as a slowly enlarging, firm, skin-coloured, pink-violet or brown **indurated plaque**, often mistaken for a scar, keloid, morphoea or DF for years, the same lesion a year apart). Later it becomes **protuberant and multinodular**.

Variants: pigmented (Bednar tumour), atrophic (looks like morphoea), and childhood/congenital forms. The the [skin cancer](condition:basal-cell-carcinoma) notes the course summary notes DFSP can **mimic a keloidal BCC**.
Deep incisional or punch biopsy that includes subcutis (shave biopsies miss it). CD34 immunohistochemistry; FISH/RT-PCR for COL1A1–PDGFB when needed.
MRI for large or recurrent tumours to define deep extent. Chest imaging only for fibrosarcomatous or metastatic disease (specialist).

differentials: DF (smaller, dimple sign), keloid/hypertrophic scar (history of injury, but beware a "keloid" that appeared without one), morphoea, lipoma, epidermoid cyst, metastasis, other sarcomas, and in children vascular malformation.

list: **IP role: suspicion and referral only.** Any "scar", "keloid" or "DF" that keeps enlarging, is >2–3 cm, or is nodular on the trunk goes to dermatology urgently (the local skin cancer or sarcoma pathway). NG12's sarcoma recommendation is a reasonable primary-care route where dermatology access is slow.

Specialist treatment: **surgery with complete peripheral and deep margin assessment** (Mohs or "slow Mohs"/staged excision with en-face margins) gives lower recurrence rates than conventional wide local excision with 2–3 cm margins, and spares tissue. European consensus (EORTC/EADO 2015, updated 2022) prefers margin-controlled surgery. Radiotherapy is for positive margins that cannot be re-excised. **Imatinib** is for unresectable or metastatic PDGFB-rearranged disease.
Follow-up: clinical, with recurrence most likely within 3–5 years.

red_flags: A ‘dermatofibroma’ or ‘keloid’ that keeps growing, is larger than about 3 cm or becomes nodular: refer to exclude **DFSP**.
pearls: "A keloid without an injury is not a keloid until proved otherwise."
Imatinib interactions (CYP3A4; warfarin; paracetamol hepatotoxicity at high doses) are worth knowing if a patient on it presents to primary care.
